falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the oxidation level, oxide distribution, and mechanical degradation (e.g., drop in ductility) are statistically indistinguishable between high-oxygen and low-oxygen exposures, or if catastrophic failure does not correlate with localized depletion of Al and Ti, the hypothesis is falsified.

hypotheses.builds_on: The paper shows that oxidation leads to elemental depletion (Al outflow) and phase transformation in related HEA systems, suggesting that selective oxidation can destabilize the microstructure.
hypotheses.what_is_new: This hypothesis applies those oxidation-induced degradation mechanisms to an fcc HEA under controlled redox conditions, focusing on the roles of both Al and Ti oxidation and linking them to catastrophic failure.

hypotheses.hypothesis: Pre-oxidation induced protective scale formation moderates degradation; absence of a stable early oxide layer permits rapid internal oxidation leading to catastrophic failure under fluctuating redox conditions.
hypotheses.material_initial_state: As-built additively manufactured Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 alloy, exhibiting a relatively defect-rich surface and uniform fcc matrix without a pre-existing protective oxide scale.
hypotheses.intervention: Perform a controlled pre-oxidation heat treatment at a lower temperature (e.g., 600–700 °C) under a mildly oxidizing atmosphere to form a thin, uniform alumina-rich surface scale prior to high-temperature exposure.
hypotheses.conditions: Subsequent exposure to cyclic elevated temperatures (above 800 °C) in oxidizing or reducing gases, where the pre-formed scale is expected to function as a barrier.
hypotheses.structural_mediator: Formation of a coherent and adherent surface oxide (primarily nano-scale alumina, possibly with contributions from TiO2) acting as a diffusion barrier.
hypotheses.mechanism: The pre-oxidation treatment promotes the early growth of a controlled, thin oxide layer that passivates the surface, limiting further rapid oxygen ingress. In untreated samples, uncontrolled oxidation leads to deeper internal oxidation, oxygen-induced embrittlement, and stress concentration that induce catastrophic failure. The intervention should demonstrate that controlling early oxide scale quality is a critical mediator of degradation.
hypotheses.predicted_outcome: Pre-oxidized samples will show a more uniform, protective oxide scale with reduced internal oxidation, slower degradation in mechanical properties, and delayed onset of catastrophic failure. In contrast, non-pre-oxidized samples will show irregular oxide penetration, increased oxidation-induced defects, and lower mechanical performance under the same conditions.
hypotheses.baseline: As-built alloy exposed directly to high-temperature redox cycling without any pre-treatment, leading to uncontrolled oxidation and early degradation.
hypotheses.boundary: Effective in environments where the oxide growth kinetics are fast (above ~800 °C) and redox cycling is present; may not be beneficial if the pre-oxidation layer spalls off due to thermal mismatches.
hypotheses.uncertainty: Adherence and long-term stability of the pre-formed oxide, and its impact on cyclic redox environments require careful experimental validation.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two groups of samples: one group receives the pre-oxidation heat treatment and one does not. Subject both groups to cyclic high-temperature exposure (>800 °C) in oxidizing/reducing environments. Compare the evolution of the oxide scale (using XRD, SEM/EDX) and mechanical integrity via high-temperature tensile or fatigue tests over time.
measurements: Surface oxide scale uniformity and composition (using XRD, SEM/EDX)
Depth of internal oxidation (cross-sectional analysis)
Mechanical property retention (tensile strength, toughness) after exposure
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If pre-oxidation does not result in a statistically significant improvement in oxide scale quality or mechanical performance compared to untreated samples, or if both groups exhibit similar catastrophic failure modes, the hypothesis is falsified.

hypotheses.builds_on: The original paper's finding that pre-treatment can lead to a protective alumina shell and improved mechanical performance is extended to an fcc HEA system under cyclic redox conditions.
hypotheses.what_is_new: This hypothesis introduces the controlled pre-oxidation processing step for an fcc high-entropy alloy to test whether an early-formed, coherent oxide scale can mitigate catastrophic failure by limiting rapid internal oxidation.

hypotheses.hypothesis: Processing-induced defects facilitate accelerated oxidation along melt pool boundaries, where localized oxidation-induced stresses combine with inherent porosity to trigger catastrophic failure under redox exposure.
hypotheses.material_initial_state: Additively manufactured Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 fabricated via laser-based powder bed fusion, featuring typical as-built defects such as micro-porosity, incomplete fusion regions, and melt-pool boundaries within the fcc matrix.
hypotheses.intervention: Apply a post-processing surface remelting or hot isostatic pressing (HIP) treatment to reduce or eliminate near-surface porosity and melt pool boundary defects in a set of samples, while keeping an untreated set as the baseline.
hypotheses.conditions: Expose both treated and untreated samples to elevated temperatures (approximately 800–1000 °C) in oxidizing or moderately reducing gas environments.
hypotheses.structural_mediator: Presence (or absence) of microstructural defects and porosity that act as fast diffusion paths for oxygen ingress, promoting localized oxidation at internal boundaries.
hypotheses.mechanism: In untreated additively manufactured samples, inherent process-induced defects and porosity provide preferential sites for oxygen diffusion. paper_did: Used a gas‐atomized FeNiCoCrMo0.5Al1.3 high‐entropy alloy powder.
Deposited coatings via HVOF spraying while varying the spraying distance to control oxidation and porosity.

Studied oxidation and phase transformations under three different thermal regimes: during HVOF deposition, by continuous heating in air (using DTA/TGA and in situ XRD), and via prolonged isothermal annealing at 800 °C.
Characterized the coatings and powders using optical/SEM microscopy, EDX, XRD, microhardness testing, and thermal analysis.
paper_reported: During HVOF spraying, high oxygen concentration and rapid heating/cooling promote in‐flight oxidation, with Al diffusing to the surface resulting in alumina formation and consequent destabilization of the BCC supersaturated solution (leading to FCC formation in Al‐depleted regions).
Increasing the spraying distance increases oxide content (mainly alumina) and porosity, which in turn lowers the coating’s microhardness.

In continuous heating tests, the BCC supersaturated solid solution decomposes (with sigma phase formation) before oxidation becomes pronounced, with oxidation commencing over 800 °C leading to additional FCC and alumina formation.

During prolonged annealing at 800 °C, a sequence of BCC decomposition, elemental diffusion (e.g., of Al, Cr, Fe, Mo), and oxidation leads to a protective alumina surface layer and an undersurface sigma‐rich layer, which ultimately affects microhardness.
paper_proposed: Employing feedstock powder with an excessive Al concentration to suppress unwanted FCC formation during deposition.
Using a preliminary heat treatment of the feedstock powder to produce a higher hardness material with a protective alumina shell for improved tribological performance.

paper_did: Produced an Al0.5CrFeNiTi high entropy alloy via powder metallurgy by mechanically alloying elemental powders (Al, Cr, Fe, Ni, Ti) in a planetary ball mill for 20 hours under an argon atmosphere using a wet milling process with n-heptane.

Processed the mechanically alloyed powder by cold pressing (200 kN force) into green compacts followed by multi-step sintering at different temperatures (750 °C, 875 °C, and 1000 °C) with varied cooling protocols.
Characterized the powders and sintered samples comprehensively using SEM, EDS, XRD, particle size distribution measurements, and density/porosity analysis.
Calculated theoretical parameters (ΔHmix, ΔSmix, δ, Ω, VEC) to predict phase stability and assess whether solid solutions or intermetallic compounds would form.
paper_reported: Demonstrated that 20 hours of mechanical alloying leads to enhanced alloying with a reduced and uniform particle size (average ~60.4 µm) and effective homogenization of constituent elements.

Found that the sintered samples developed a compact structure with identified FCC, BCC, and HCP phases (with key peaks at specific 2θ positions) and that sintering conditions influence pore size and overall consolidation.

Observed only slight oxidation due to processing under inert conditions and confirmed that the experimental phase distribution was consistent with theoretical predictions (e.g., via VEC calculations).
paper_proposed: Suggested that further processing methods should be explored to reduce the porosity of the bulk material and further optimize properties for practical applications.

hypotheses.hypothesis: Grain Boundary Oxidation Governs Degradation: In an oxidizing atmosphere at elevated temperatures, oxygen preferentially diffuses along the grain boundaries of the additively manufactured Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 alloy (with an fcc matrix), promoting the formation of brittle oxide phases (primarily based on Cr and Al). These continuous intergranular oxide films eventually compromise cohesive strength and lead to catastrophic failure. A controlled pre-oxidation treatment that forms a thin, uniform, and adherent passivating oxide scale could block rapid oxygen ingress along the boundaries.

hypotheses.structural_mediator: Grain boundary oxide film thickness and continuity.
hypotheses.mechanism: The pre-formed passivating oxide scale impedes rapid oxygen penetration along grain boundaries, reducing the formation of thick, brittle intergranular oxides that would otherwise weaken the matrix. In untreated samples, uncontrolled boundary oxidation leads to intergranular embrittlement and crack propagation.
hypotheses.predicted_outcome: Pre-oxidized samples will exhibit slower degradation rates, fewer intergranular cracks, and a delayed onset of catastrophic failure compared to untreated samples.
hypotheses.baseline: As-built alloy with no pre-oxidation, which under oxidizing high-temperature exposure rapidly develops grain boundary oxidation and associated mechanical weakening.
hypotheses.boundary: Effective in oxidizing environments at temperatures sufficient to promote oxidation but where the pre-oxidized scale remains stable (e.g., 800–1000 °C); it may be less effective if temperature or oxygen partial pressure exceeds the stability limits of the passivating film.
hypotheses.uncertainty: While the qualitative improvement is expected, the magnitude of degradation rate reduction is uncertain without experimental quantification.

This reduction triggers the formation of internal voids and pores beneath the surface, which coalesce over time leading to loss of mechanical integrity and eventual catastrophic failure. paper_did: Fabricated equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi high‐entropy alloy (HEA) using selective laser melting (SLM) with pre‐alloyed powder under controlled processing parameters.

Conducted extensive microstructural characterization (SEM, EBSD, XRD, TEM, ECC imaging) to confirm a single FCC phase, epitaxial growth grains, fine cellular/columnar structures decorated with dislocation networks, and the presence of nano‐sized Mn2O3 precipitates.

Performed room‐ and high‐temperature compressive mechanical tests (from 25 °C up to ~900 °C) to elucidate deformation mechanisms such as slip, deformation twinning (up to 600 °C), and dynamic recrystallization along with dynamic recovery (above 700 °C).
paper_reported: SLM‐built equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi HEA exhibited outstanding mechanical properties across a wide temperature range, with high yield strength attributed to its fine grain size, high dislocation density (~1.88×10^14 m⁻²), and nano‐sized Mn2O3 precipitates.

Distinct deformation mechanisms were identified: slip and deformation twinning dominated from room temperature to 600 °C, while above 700 °C a combination of slip with partial recrystallization (with contributions from both discontinuous and geometric DRX) led to flow softening.

The study interpreted multiple strengthening contributions – including dislocation forest hardening and Orowan strengthening by nano‐oxides – and noted that the Zener pinning effect of oxides and migrated grain boundaries delays full recrystallization at high temperatures.
paper_proposed: That correlations among microstructural features (grain structure, dislocation networks, nano‐oxide dispersions) and temperature‐dependent properties can be exploited to tailor mechanical performance.
That adjustments to SLM processing parameters (for example, scanning strategies) may control texture evolution and thereby optimize strength and ductility.
A direction for future work to further explore the interplay between unique microstructural states (especially the role of nano‐oxides) and high‐temperature deformation mechanisms.

hypotheses.hypothesis: Under oxidizing conditions at high temperature, the catastrophic failure of additively manufactured Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 arises from the formation of a continuous, brittle oxide scale (rich in Ti- and possibly Al-oxides) along grain boundaries, which promotes intergranular cracking and eventual failure.
hypotheses.material_initial_state: As-built, SLM-produced Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 HEA with an FCC matrix featuring a fine grain structure, high dislocation density, and nano-sized oxide particles formed during processing.
hypotheses.intervention: Apply a controlled pre-oxidation heat treatment in a mildly oxidizing environment to promote the formation of a coherent, protective thin oxide layer prior to high-temperature exposure.
hypotheses.conditions: Elevated temperatures between 700 °C and 900 °C under oxidizing gas conditions (e.g., controlled O2 partial pressure).
hypotheses.structural_mediator: Grain boundary oxide scale thickness and coherence; intergranular oxide particle distribution.
hypotheses.mechanism: At high temperatures, the fast diffusion of Ti and Al leads to the growth of a continuous brittle oxide film along the grain boundaries. In the untreated (as-built) state, the nano-oxides are small and finely dispersed, contributing to strength. However, exposure to an oxidizing atmosphere causes these oxides to coalesce into a thicker scale that weakens the grain boundaries via embrittlement. The controlled pre-oxidation treatment can promote a more protective, adherent thin scale that mitigates further oxidation, thereby delaying or preventing catastrophic intergranular failure.
hypotheses.predicted_outcome: Compared to untreated samples, pre-oxidized samples should exhibit a slower rate of strength degradation, fewer intergranular cracks, and delayed catastrophic failure under oxidizing high-temperature exposure. The protective oxide layer should be observable via TEM/SEM in cross-sectional analysis.
hypotheses.baseline: As-built alloy exposed to oxidizing conditions shows rapid formation of thick brittle oxides at grain boundaries leading to early failure.
hypotheses.boundary: Tested at temperatures between 700 °C and 900 °C with controlled oxygen levels; outside these boundaries the oxidation kinetics may differ.
hypotheses.uncertainty: While the role of nano-oxides is evident in the paper (e.g., PMC7229066::web::010, PMC7229066::web::016), quantitative details of oxide scale evolution in this non-equiatomic alloy under controlled pre-oxidation are less established.

hypotheses.intervention: Conduct a controlled comparison by exposing samples to either an oxidizing or a reducing gas environment at high temperature, while incorporating in-situ compositional analysis at grain boundaries with minimal pre-deformation.
hypotheses.conditions: Exposure at 750–900 °C in a reducing atmosphere (e.g., H2-rich gas mixture) versus an oxidizing atmosphere.
hypotheses.structural_mediator: Grain boundary composition and segregation; presence or absence of protective oxides.
hypotheses.mechanism: In a reducing environment, the absence of oxygen prevents the formation of a stable oxide scale, thereby favoring the selective reduction (or even evaporation) of certain elements such as Ti or Cr at the grain boundaries. This selective loss or redistribution can cause local compositional gradients that weaken grain boundary cohesion, leading to premature intergranular failure. In contrast, oxidizing conditions might at least form a continuous oxide that, albeit brittle, maintains some barrier integrity.

hypotheses.uncertainty: While compositional segregation under oxidative conditions is well documented in some HEAs, the specific behavior under reducing conditions for this composition is less established and might involve complex kinetics.

pool.label: C1
pool.builds_on: The paper’s findings on high-energy grain boundaries and rapid degradation pathways in additively manufactured HEAs are extended by a deliberate pre-oxidation strategy to form a protective interface.
pool.what_is_new: This hypothesis proposes an intentional pre-oxidation step to engineer a passivating Al–Cr–Ti rich oxide film, a controlled surface treatment not investigated in the paper, to mitigate gas-assisted degradation.

fields.hypothesis: A controlled pre-oxidation treatment can form an ultrathin, adherent mixed oxide film enriched in Al, Cr, and Ti on the surface and along near‐surface grain boundaries, passivating high-energy sites and blocking reactive gas ingress during high-temperature exposure, thereby delaying localized degradation and catastrophic failure.
fields.material_initial_state: As-built SLM Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 HEA having a fine-grained FCC matrix with high-energy grain boundaries, inherent nano‐scale porosity, and residual stresses.
fields.intervention: Expose the as-built samples to a controlled pre-oxidation treatment at approximately 400 °C for 30 minutes in a low oxygen partial pressure (e.g., a diluted O2/Ar mixture) to generate a protective, nano-scale oxide film.
fields.conditions: After pre-oxidation, subject the samples to elevated-temperature exposures (600–800 °C) under oxidizing or reducing gas environments and cyclic mechanical loading conditions to simulate service.
fields.structural_mediator: Formation of a continuous, ultrathin oxide film (comprising primarily Al2O3, Cr2O3, and possibly titania phases) at the surface and penetrating shallowly along grain boundaries that hinders gas permeation.
fields.mechanism: The pre-formed oxide film effectively passivates high-energy sites along grain boundaries by reducing chemical activity and blocking rapid diffusion channels for reactive gas species. This barrier reduces the localized oxidation or reduction reactions that would otherwise weaken grain boundary cohesion and initiate catastrophic failure.
fields.predicted_outcome: Pre-oxidized samples are expected to exhibit shallower depths of gas-induced degradation, fewer intergranular attack sites, and an improved fatigue life (on the order of tens of percent improvement, if the passivation remains robust under cyclic loading) compared to untreated samples.
fields.baseline: As-built HEA specimens without pre-oxidation, which under high-temperature reactive gas exposure form deep, uncontrolled degradation along high-energy grain boundaries leading to early crack initiation.
fields.boundary: This approach is applicable at elevated temperature exposures between 600 °C and 800 °C where the protective oxide remains thermodynamically stable; the pre-oxidation treatment must be carefully tuned to avoid formation of thick, brittle oxide layers.
fields.uncertainty: Moderate uncertainty exists regarding the long-term adhesion and mechanical durability of the ultrathin film under cyclic loading at high temperatures.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two groups of as-built SLM HEA samples. Subject one group to the pre-oxidation treatment (400 °C for 30 minutes in a low O2/Ar atmosphere) and leave the other group untreated. Expose both groups to a reactive gas environment (oxidizing or reducing) at 700 °C under cyclic loading. Use cross-sectional TEM, XPS, and EDS to assess the oxide film integrity and degradation penetration, and perform cyclic fatigue tests to record cycles to failure.
measurements: Oxide film thickness, composition, and continuity (TEM, XPS)
Depth of gas-induced degradation along grain boundaries (TEM/EDS)
Cyclic fatigue life at 700 °C
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the pre-oxidized samples do not show at least a 20% improvement in degradation metrics (reduced penetration depth) and cyclic fatigue life compared to untreated samples, the hypothesis is refuted.

pool.label: C2
pool.builds_on: It leverages the concept that grain boundaries in HEAs can serve as fast diffusion paths for degrading species, extending it by engineering protective nano-dispersoids via controlled oxygen exposure—a mechanism not explored in the original paper.
pool.what_is_new: This hypothesis introduces a novel process modulation (controlled oxygen doping) during/after SLM to induce beneficial nano-oxide precipitate formation, offering an internal microstructural barrier to gas diffusion not previously addressed.

fields.hypothesis: Introducing a controlled oxygen presence during or immediately after SLM processing will induce in situ formation of nano-dispersed oxide precipitates (e.g., Al2O3 and TiO2) preferentially at grain boundaries, which then act as effective diffusion barriers to reactive gas species during high-temperature exposure, thereby retarding degradation and catastrophic failure.
fields.material_initial_state: As-built SLM Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 HEA with a fine FCC microstructure characterized by high dislocation densities, residual nano-porosity, and unmodified grain boundaries.
fields.intervention: Modify the processing/post-processing atmosphere by introducing a controlled, very low oxygen partial pressure (e.g., ~0.1% O2 in the processing gas) for a brief period near the end of the SLM process or during a post-build treatment to promote the nucleation of nano-oxide dispersoids at grain boundaries.
fields.conditions: Following this oxygen-doping treatment, expose the samples to oxidizing or reducing gas environments at elevated temperatures (600–800 °C) while subjecting them to cyclic loading conditions.
fields.structural_mediator: Formation of a uniform dispersion of stable, nano-scale oxide precipitates (primarily Al2O3 and TiO2) along grain boundaries and within the matrix that impede fast diffusion channels.
fields.mechanism: The presence of finely dispersed oxide particles at grain boundaries will hinder the rapid transport of reactive gas species along the high-diffusivity paths by physically obstructing diffusion and by pinning dislocations. This limits the local chemical reactions that degrade boundary cohesion and delays crack nucleation and propagation under high-temperature conditions.
fields.predicted_outcome: Oxygen-doped samples with nano-oxide dispersoids will show reduced degradation penetration depths and improved fatigue performance under cyclic high-temperature exposure relative to samples processed entirely in an oxygen-free environment. The magnitude of improvement is expected to be moderate, though exact values are uncertain.
fields.baseline: Standard as-built HEA samples produced in nearly inert (oxygen-free) conditions, which lack the protective nano-scale oxide distribution and thus exhibit faster gas penetration and earlier catastrophic failure.
fields.boundary: This strategy is effective only if the oxygen level is precisely controlled to produce nano-oxides rather than coarse or continuous oxide films. The treatment is applicable within the 600–800 °C exposure range where oxide stability is maintained.
fields.uncertainty: There is moderate uncertainty regarding the nucleation kinetics of nano-oxides in the complex multi-component alloy and the balance between beneficial precipitation and potential embrittlement.

falsification_experiment.design: Process two groups of HEA samples: one group under standard inert atmosphere and another with a controlled oxygen addition (≈0.1% O2) during the final processing stage. Characterize grain-boundary regions via TEM/EDS for nano-oxide precipitates. Subsequently, expose both groups to a reactive gas environment at 700 °C under cyclic loading and compare degradation features and fatigue life.
measurements: Nano-oxide size, distribution, and composition at grain boundaries (TEM/EDS)
Degradation penetration depth (cross-sectional TEM)
Fatigue life under cyclic high-temperature exposure
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the oxygen-doped samples do not exhibit a statistically significant (≥20%) reduction in degradation features and an improvement in fatigue life compared to the inert-processed controls, the hypothesis is refuted.

pool.label: C3
pool.builds_on: The paper’s documentation of diffusion-driven intergranular σ‐phase and nitride growth in SLM HEAs, combined with established principles of grain boundary pinning to control diffusion in alloys.
pool.what_is_new: This hypothesis proposes a specific alloy modification (minor Zr addition) to tailor the grain boundary chemistry and structure, thereby actively impeding the diffusion-controlled embrittlement mechanism – an approach not examined in the original study.

fields.hypothesis: Under reducing high-temperature conditions, degradation and catastrophic failure are governed by intergranular coarsening of brittle σ‐phase and nitride precipitates due to uninhibited diffusion along high-energy grain boundaries. A minor alloy modification that introduces a grain-boundary pinning element (e.g., zirconium) can suppress this diffusion-driven coarsening and enhance high-temperature mechanical stability.
fields.material_initial_state: SLM-fabricated Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 alloy with its as-built FCC matrix containing fine σ‐phase precursors and nitrides, along with a columnar grain structure characteristic of SLM processes.
fields.intervention: Introduce a minor amount of zirconium (e.g., 0.5–1 at.%) either via alloying during powder preparation or through surface doping that preferentially segregates to grain boundaries.
fields.conditions: Exposure to reducing gas atmospheres (e.g., hydrogen-containing or inert-reducing environments) at elevated temperatures (~950–1100 K) where diffusion-controlled intergranular growth is active.
fields.structural_mediator: The formation of Zr-rich precipitates or segregated Zr at grain boundaries that acts as a pinning agent, thus reducing the mobility of atoms involved in σ‐phase and nitride coarsening.
fields.mechanism: Zirconium additions can segregate to the grain boundaries and form fine, thermally stable dispersoids that hinder long-range diffusion along these boundaries. This pinning effect limits the coarsening and growth of embrittling σ‐phase and nitride precipitates, preserving grain boundary integrity. In a reducing environment, where external oxidation is minimal, such diffusion control is critical for maintaining mechanical performance.
fields.predicted_outcome: Zr-modified samples should demonstrate a finer, more stable grain-boundary microstructure with reduced precipitate coarsening. These samples are expected to exhibit improved high-temperature ductility and delayed catastrophic failure compared to conventionally alloyed samples.
fields.baseline: Standard as-built samples without Zr addition, which under prolonged reducing exposure at high temperature are prone to significant intergranular coarsening of σ‐phase and nitride precipitates leading to embrittlement and early failure.
fields.boundary: This approach is specifically applicable under reducing atmosphere conditions at temperatures around 950–1100 K, where diffusion along grain boundaries is the dominant degradation mechanism.
fields.uncertainty: The exact concentration of Zr required to achieve optimal grain boundary pinning without adversely affecting other alloy properties remains to be determined.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two batches of samples: one with the standard composition and another with the minor Zr addition. Expose both batches to a reducing gas environment at 1000 K for a prolonged duration.
measurements: Use EBSD and SEM to analyze grain boundary structure and quantify σ‐phase/nitride precipitate size and distribution.
Conduct high-temperature mechanical tests (e.g., microhardness and tensile strength) to evaluate degradation.
Perform compositional mapping at grain boundaries using EDS.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the Zr-doped samples do not show statistically significant suppression of intergranular precipitate coarsening and do not exhibit improved mechanical performance compared to the standard samples, the hypothesis must be rejected.

pool.label: C4
pool.builds_on: The recognition in the paper that SLM processing induces high residual stresses and dense dislocation networks—which are known to promote premature phase transformations—and established principles of stress relief in additive manufacturing.
pool.what_is_new: This hypothesis introduces the concept of a targeted subcritical annealing treatment to relieve residual stresses as a means to limit stress-assisted degradation mechanisms, thereby addressing an aspect of failure that the paper did not focus on.

fields.hypothesis: Catastrophic failure under both oxidizing and reducing conditions is accelerated by residual tensile stresses inherent to the SLM process that promote stress-assisted nucleation and growth of brittle intergranular phases. A controlled subcritical annealing treatment designed to relieve these residual stresses—without triggering significant grain growth or phase coarsening—should mitigate stress-driven degradation and delay catastrophic failure.
fields.material_initial_state: As-built additively manufactured Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 HEA displaying a characteristic SLM microstructure with columnar grains, a high density of dislocations, and significant residual tensile stresses alongside fine-scale secondary precipitates.
fields.intervention: Implement a subcritical annealing treatment (e.g., 800 K for 1–2 hours in an inert atmosphere) immediately post-fabrication to relax residual stresses while preserving the fine microstructural features.
fields.conditions: Subsequent prolonged exposure to elevated temperatures (approximately 950–1100 K) in either oxidizing or reducing environments where both diffusion-driven phase transformations and stress-assisted microcracking are active.
fields.structural_mediator: A reduction in residual tensile stresses, leading to a lower driving force for stress-assisted nucleation and coarsening of intergranular brittle phases such as σ‐phase and nitrides.
fields.mechanism: The inherent high residual stresses from the rapid solidification of the SLM process act as local driving forces for the nucleation and accelerated growth of brittle intergranular phases. A carefully designed low-temperature annealing treatment can relieve these stresses without promoting undesirable grain growth or excessive diffusive transformations. Stress relaxation decreases the likelihood of microcrack formation at grain boundaries and delays the coarsening of embrittling phases, thereby improving high-temperature performance.
fields.predicted_outcome: Samples that undergo the subcritical annealing treatment should show reduced residual stress levels (as measured by XRD or other stress analysis techniques), a lower density of stress-induced microcracks, and a more stable intergranular microstructure. These changes are expected to translate into improved high-temperature toughness and delayed onset of catastrophic failure relative to untreated samples.
fields.baseline: As-built SLM samples characterized by high residual tensile stresses and a microstructure prone to stress-assisted premature phase coarsening and crack initiation during high-temperature exposure.
fields.boundary: The stress relief approach is applicable for service exposures at temperatures from about 950 K up to 1100 K, where both diffusion and mechanical stress contribute to degradation.
fields.uncertainty: The optimum annealing parameters (temperature, duration, and atmosphere) for maximum stress relief without adverse microstructural coarsening need to be empirically determined.

falsification_experiment.design: Divide samples into two groups: one group receives the subcritical annealing treatment (800 K for 1–2 hours in an inert atmosphere) and the other is left in the as-built condition. Both groups are then subjected to prolonged high-temperature exposure (1000 K) in either oxidizing or reducing atmospheres.
measurements: Evaluate residual stresses using X-ray diffraction or similar methods before and after treatment.
Use SEM/EBSD to assess microstructural evolution, particularly the formation and coarsening of intergranular precipitates and microcrack density.
Perform high-temperature mechanical testing to compare toughness and strength.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the annealed samples do not exhibit a significant reduction in residual stresses, lower microcrack density, and improved mechanical performance compared to the as-built samples after high-temperature exposure, the hypothesis is falsified.

pool.label: C5
pool.builds_on: the paper’s findings (PMC9026100) that high surface free energy and the formation of protective layers (chromia and alumina) in refined microstructures are linked to oxidation resistance.
pool.what_is_new: Introduces an engineered pre-oxidation surface modification to deliberately seed protective oxidation, rather than relying solely on microstructural refinement via thermomechanical processing.

fields.hypothesis: A pre-oxidation surface modification via deposition of a thin, reactive Al-rich coating will seed formation of a continuous protective alumina/chromia scale, thereby reducing deleterious spinel formation and mitigating catastrophic failure during high-temperature exposure.
fields.material_initial_state: Additively manufactured Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 HEA with an fcc matrix, exhibiting a native surface with a high density of active sites (high surface free energy) that under standard conditions may develop mixed oxide scales including non-protective spinels.
fields.intervention: Deposit a ~100-nm thick Al-rich coating (e.g., via laser cladding or sputtering) on the AM samples prior to high-temperature exposure.
fields.conditions: Elevated-temperature exposure (850–1050 °C) in controlled oxidizing atmospheres for long-term oxidation testing (e.g., 100 h).
fields.structural_mediator: Modified surface chemistry that predefines the nucleation sites and enhances the formation of a uniform alumina and/or chromia layer.
fields.mechanism: The deposited Al-rich layer enhances local Al availability at the surface, promoting the formation of a continuous, adherent alumina scale that suppresses the nucleation of non-protective spinel oxides. By controlling the early-stage oxidation chemistry, oxygen diffusion is better regulated, reducing internal oxidation and crack formation that may lead to catastrophic degradation. This approach builds on the idea from PMC9026100 that protective oxide patches are closely linked to surface composition and free energy.
fields.predicted_outcome: Coated samples should exhibit lower overall mass gain (by about 30–50% relative to baseline), show a more uniform and crack-free oxide scale, and a delay in catastrophic failure onset under high-temperature oxidation.
fields.baseline: Uncoated AM HEA samples that tend to form a mixed oxide scale with deleterious formation of non-protective spinel phases and a higher incidence of oxide cracking.
fields.boundary: Effective primarily under oxidizing conditions at temperatures where alumina formation is thermodynamically favored (850–1050 °C); may be less effective in highly reducing environments.
fields.uncertainty: Moderate; while surface modifications to control oxidation are established in other systems, the quantitative performance in HEAs, especially under cyclic thermal conditions, will need determination.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of AM HEA samples, one with the Al-rich coating and a control group without coating. Subject both groups to identical oxidation cycles at 900 °C in an oxidizing environment for 100 h and then analyze oxide scale composition, continuity (via XRD and SEM/EDS), and measure cumulative mass gain.
measurements: XRD phase identification of oxide scale
SEM/EDS characterization of scale morphology and crack density
Mass gain measurements
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the coated samples do not form a more continuous and protective alumina/chromia scale and show no reduction in mass gain or delay in cracking compared to the control, then the hypothesis is falsified.

pool.label: C6
pool.builds_on: The paper’s observation that phase segregation and deleterious precipitate formation (e.g., Cr-rich particles) can govern degradation mechanisms at high temperatures, extended here to a different alloy system and substituting the role of Mn with Ti segregation effects.
pool.what_is_new: This hypothesis introduces the idea that additive manufacturing–induced microsegregation (specifically of Ti) plays a dominant role in the oxidation degradation and catastrophic failure under high-temperature oxidizing exposures, and that controlled homogenization can mitigate this effect.

fields.hypothesis: Degradation and catastrophic failure are governed by intergranular oxidation induced by Ti segregation. In additively manufactured Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3, residual microsegregation of Ti to grain boundaries promotes the formation of discrete, brittle TiO2 particles during elevated‐temperature oxidation. Their presence weakens grain boundary cohesion, leading to intergranular crack initiation and propagation under cyclic thermal and mechanical stresses.
fields.material_initial_state: Additively manufactured, as-built Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 HEA with an FCC matrix and typical microsegregation (including Ti enrichment at grain boundaries) due to rapid solidification.
fields.intervention: Apply a post-build homogenization annealing treatment at a moderate temperature (e.g., 900–1000 °C) designed to reduce Ti segregation at grain boundaries without fully coarsening the microstructure.
fields.conditions: Elevated-temperature exposure (e.g., 700–800 °C) in an oxidizing gas atmosphere (e.g., air) for extended durations (hundreds of hours), with cyclic thermal loads to simulate service conditions.
fields.structural_mediator: Grain-boundary chemistry and oxide precipitate distribution (specifically, reduction or spatial homogenization of Ti-rich regions).
fields.mechanism: In the as-built state, local enrichment of Ti at grain boundaries promotes the nucleation of TiO2 during oxidative exposure. The resulting brittle oxide particles disrupt the cohesiveness of grain boundaries. Annealing reduces the segregation, leading to a more homogeneous distribution of Ti and thus forms a more uniform, less disruptive oxide scale. As a result, the likelihood of intergranular cracking, which can lead to catastrophic failure, is reduced.
fields.predicted_outcome: Annealed samples will exhibit a more uniform, adherent oxide scale with fewer intergranular cracks, and a significant delay (or reduction) in catastrophic failure compared to as-built samples. The magnitude of improvement is expected qualitatively; quantitative predictions are uncertain.
fields.baseline: As-built additive manufactured microstructure with grain-boundary Ti segregation leading to early intergranular oxidation and rapid crack propagation under oxidizing conditions.
fields.boundary: Effective below temperatures where full homogenization and grain growth do not occur (i.e., maintain FCC matrix stability) and within oxidizing gas conditions.
fields.uncertainty: Exact kinetics of Ti segregation/redistribution and the precise improvement in failure strain under service cyclic loads.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 samples: one in the as-built state and one given the proposed homogenization anneal. Expose both sets to 750 °C in an air atmosphere for 500 hours with thermal cycling. Analyze grain-boundary chemistry using electron microscopy and assess crack density and oxide scale adherence.
measurements: Grain-boundary composition (via EDS/TEM)
Crack density and intergranular crack length measurements
Adhesion and continuity of oxide scale (via SEM)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the annealed samples do not show reduced Ti segregation, lower crack density, or improved oxide scale adhesion relative to as-built samples, the hypothesis is falsified.

pool.label: C7
pool.builds_on: The paper discusses how protective oxide layers (e.g., Cr2O3) can mitigate elemental dissolution in corrosive environments. Here, that concept is extended to an alloy system where both Al and Cr contribute to a protective mixed oxide, with a focus on mitigating the effects of microstructural heterogeneities from additive manufacturing.
pool.what_is_new: It proposes a proactive surface pre-treatment to engineer the oxide scale prior to high-temperature exposure, a strategy not explored in the paper, to control degradation and prevent catastrophic failure.

fields.hypothesis: The degradation is controlled by the evolution and integrity of a protective mixed oxide scale, primarily based on Al and Cr oxidation. In the as-built Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 HEA, local microstructural heterogeneities limit continuous passivating oxide formation. Catastrophic failure ensues from localized oxide spallation and internal oxidation when the protective layer is discontinuous.
fields.material_initial_state: Additively manufactured Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 HEA with an FCC matrix exhibiting intrinsic microstructural heterogeneities (e.g., variations in elemental distributions and porosity) that can impair uniform oxide formation.
fields.intervention: Implement a controlled pre-oxidation treatment at a lower temperature (e.g., 600 °C in a controlled oxygen partial pressure environment) prior to high-temperature exposure to promote the formation of a continuous, adherent Al2O3/Cr2O3 mixed oxide scale.
fields.conditions: Initial pre-oxidation in a mildly oxidizing gas (with controlled oxygen partial pressure) followed by high-temperature exposure at 700–800 °C in either oxidizing or reducing gases, to simulate service conditions.
fields.structural_mediator: Oxide scale microstructure and adhesion quality at the alloy’s surface.
fields.mechanism: A pre-established, coherent oxide scale based on the oxidation of Al and Cr acts as a diffusion barrier to oxygen and prevents deleterious internal oxidation. Without pre-oxidation, heterogeneity in the as-built microstructure leads to discontinuities in the oxide layer, resulting in localized oxidation attack, loss of mechanical integrity, and ultimately catastrophic failure.
fields.predicted_outcome: Pre-oxidized samples will exhibit a uniform, adherent, and continuous oxide scale, leading to a reduced degradation rate and delayed onset of catastrophic failure compared to untreated samples. The improvement is expected to be notably visible (e.g., reduced oxide spallation and lower oxidation depth).
fields.baseline: Untreated as-built HEA samples that form patchy oxide scales with areas of localized internal oxidation, leading to microcracking and progressive structural degradation.
fields.boundary: Effects are expected under elevated-temperature exposures in both oxidizing and moderately reducing gas atmospheres, provided the oxygen partial pressure during pre-oxidation is controlled.
fields.uncertainty: The precise thickness and composition of the optimal pre-formed scale and the quantitative relationship between pre-oxidation parameters and long-term oxidation resistance.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of samples: one with the proposed low-temperature pre-oxidation treatment and one as-built. Expose both to high-temperature (750 °C) oxidizing gas environments for 500 hours. Characterize the oxide scale continuity and adhesion using surface analysis (SEM, XRD) and monitor for signs of spallation or internal oxidation.
measurements: Oxide scale continuity and phase identification (XRD/SEM)
Spallation rate (mass change after thermal cycling)
Cross-sectional imaging to measure oxide thickness
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If pre-oxidized samples do not show a statistically significant improvement in oxide scale integrity or delayed catastrophic failure compared to untreated samples, the hypothesis is falsified.

pool.label: C8
pool.builds_on: The original paper indicated that a protective oxide film improves high-temperature wear behavior (PMC7515071::web::011–012). This hypothesis leverages that observation by intentionally pre-forming the protective layer.
pool.what_is_new: It introduces a deliberate pre-oxidation step to engineer the oxide scale before service, a processing route distinct from those studied in SPS samples and addressing the specific challenges of AM-produced FCC HEAs.

fields.hypothesis: Pre-Oxidation Heat Treatment Induces a Uniform, Protective Passivation Layer That Mitigates Catastrophic Oxidation
fields.material_initial_state: As-built additively manufactured Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 HEA featuring rough surface topographies and microstructural inhomogeneities typical of AM processes.
fields.intervention: Apply a controlled pre-oxidation (passivation) heat treatment, for example, holding the material at a moderate temperature (600–650 °C) in static air for 1–2 hours to form a thin, well-adherent oxide layer.
fields.conditions: Following pre-oxidation, expose the samples to high-temperature environments (850–900 °C) under both oxidizing and reducing atmospheres for extended times (e.g., 5 hours).
fields.structural_mediator: Formation of a pre-formed, uniform, dense oxide (passivation) layer that acts as an oxygen ingress barrier.
fields.mechanism: A pre-oxidation treatment permits the development of a thin, continuous oxide scale that is more uniform than the native oxide immediately generated during service. This pre-formed layer limits rapid oxygen diffusion along preferential pathways (e.g., surface irregularities or grain boundaries) during subsequent high-temperature exposure. As a result, it reduces the formation of thick, discontinuous oxide scales and minimizes stress concentrations that can lead to spallation and eventual catastrophic failure.
fields.predicted_outcome: Pre-oxidized samples will show a more controlled oxide scale buildup during subsequent high-temperature exposure, with a lower rate of oxide spallation and less mechanical degradation (e.g., wear or crack formation) compared to as-built samples.
fields.baseline: As-built AM HEA samples with no pre-treatment, which form native oxide scales during high-temperature exposure that may be less uniform.
fields.boundary: This effect should be most significant at temperatures where oxidation is rapid (≥850 °C) and when the exposure time is sufficient for further oxide growth; at lower temperatures the pre-formed layer’s impact may be limited.
fields.uncertainty: The optimal pre-oxidation conditions (temperature, time) necessary to produce an ideal passivating layer for this alloy are not precisely known and may require further optimization.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of AM HEA samples: one set left as-built and one set subjected to a pre-oxidation heat treatment (600–650 °C for 1–2 hours). Then expose both sets to 850–900 °C under ambient air and a mildly reducing atmosphere for 5 hours. Evaluate oxide scale morphology (via SEM/EDS), measure oxide thickness evolution and perform mechanical tests (e.g., microhardness or wear resistance tests).
measurements: Uniformity and thickness of the oxide scale via microscopy
Chemical composition mapping of the oxide layer
Mechanical performance metrics during high-temperature exposure
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the pre-oxidized samples do not exhibit significantly improved oxide scale uniformity and corresponding mechanical stability when compared with as-built samples under identical high-temperature conditions, then the hypothesis is falsified.

pool.label: C9
pool.builds_on: The paper’s findings of heterogeneous oxide formation and spallation (PMC8346963::web::007) and literature linking microstructural uniformity to improved oxidation resistance (TXT::wikipedia::Stainless_steel::028).
pool.what_is_new: This hypothesis tests the effect of a post-processing densification (via HIP) on the oxidation behavior of additively manufactured Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 HEA—a strategy not investigated in the original paper—to mitigate localized defects that act as initiation sites for catastrophic oxidation failure.

fields.hypothesis: Post‐processing via Hot Isostatic Pressing (HIP) reduces internal porosity and microstructural defects, leading to more uniform oxide scale formation during high‐temperature oxidation and thereby delaying catastrophic failure.
fields.material_initial_state: As‐built additively manufactured Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 HEA that typically exhibits residual porosity, microstructural defects, and heterogeneous grain structure due to the layer‐by‐layer melting process.
fields.intervention: Subject the as‐built samples to a HIP treatment (e.g., at ~800 °C under an appropriate isostatic pressure for several hours) to densify the material and relieve residual stresses prior to oxidation testing.
fields.conditions: After HIP treatment, expose the samples to elevated temperatures (700–900 °C) in synthetic air for durations up to 48 hours.
fields.structural_mediator: A densified, nearly defect‐free microstructure diminishes localized oxygen ingress and uneven oxide nucleation at defects and porosity, fostering the formation of a more coherent oxide scale.
fields.mechanism: Eliminating or reducing microstructural defects and porosity through HIP minimizes pathways for rapid oxygen diffusion and localized oxide overgrowth. The resulting uniformity in the substrate promotes a more even, protective oxide scale that resists spallation, thereby delaying failure.
fields.predicted_outcome: HIP-treated samples will exhibit lower mass gain, a more uniform and adherent oxide layer (as observed through SEM), and reduced crack/void density compared to untreated, as-built samples when exposed to 900 °C.
fields.baseline: The as‐built alloy with inherent porosity and defect sites that promote uneven oxidation and rapid localized degradation leading to catastrophic spallation.
fields.boundary: Effective within the temperature range of 700–900 °C in oxidizing environments; if HIP induces detrimental grain growth or other microstructural issues at higher temperatures, the outcome might vary.
fields.uncertainty: While HIP is known to reduce porosity and improve mechanical performance, the optimal HIP parameters for this specific HEA to beneficially influence oxidation behavior remain to be established.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of samples: one as-built and one HIP-treated under defined parameters. Expose both sets to 900 °C in synthetic air for 24 and 48 hours. Analyze oxide scale uniformity, porosity, and crack density using SEM and measure mass gain kinetics.
measurements: Microstructural density and porosity (SEM, possibly X-ray computed tomography)
Oxide scale morphology and adherence (cross-sectional SEM, EDS)
Gravimetric mass gain data
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If HIP-treated samples do not exhibit statistically significant improvements in oxide scale uniformity (reduced cracks and voids) and lower mass gain compared to as-built samples, the hypothesis is falsified.

pool.label: C10
pool.builds_on: The paper noted that adding Ni in similar HEA systems improved oxidation resistance by reducing Cr2O3 volatility (PMC8346963::web::005), and literature on superalloys highlights the stabilizing effect of Ni on protective oxide scales (TXT::wikipedia::Superalloy::002).
pool.what_is_new: This hypothesis introduces a controlled surface alloying approach (via pack cementation) to deliberately enrich Ni at the surface, thereby engineering the formation of a more protective oxide scale on the additively manufactured HEA—a strategy not explored in the original study.

fields.hypothesis: A surface enrichment of Ni via a controlled pack cementation process stabilizes the formation of a protective Cr2O3-based spinel layer, thereby reducing oxide volatility and spallation that lead to catastrophic failure.
fields.material_initial_state: As‐built Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 HEA with a uniform bulk composition but without deliberate surface modification to enhance the formation of stable oxide layers.
fields.intervention: Apply a pack cementation treatment to create a thin, Ni-enriched surface layer. This process involves embedding samples in a powder mixture containing Ni precursors and activating agents, followed by a brief high-temperature treatment to promote Ni diffusion into the surface.
fields.conditions: After surface treatment, expose samples to elevated temperatures (700–900 °C) in synthetic air for up to 48 hours.
fields.structural_mediator: The Ni-enriched surface modifies the oxidation kinetics by facilitating the formation of a continuous, adherent Cr2O3-based spinel (Ni–Cr mixed oxide) that acts as a robust diffusion barrier.
fields.mechanism: Additional surface Ni can reduce the volatility of Cr2O3 by forming a stable, mixed oxide spinel phase. This phase offers improved adherence and mechanical integrity, thereby reducing oxygen ingress and the formation of disruptive voids, which in turn delays the onset of catastrophic failure.
fields.predicted_outcome: Pack cementation-treated samples will show slower oxidation kinetics (lower mass gain), a more coherent and protective oxide layer with fewer voids and cracks, and delayed catastrophic failure compared to untreated samples under identical high-temperature oxidizing conditions.
fields.baseline: As-built samples with nominal composition that develop oxide scales which may include less adherent and more volatile oxide phases, leading to spallation at elevated temperatures as observed in the paper.
fields.boundary: The effect is expected to be significant within the temperature range of 700–900 °C in synthetic air. The influence of such surface enrichment under different atmospheres or at temperatures outside this range is not addressed.
fields.uncertainty: Although literature supports Ni’s role in stabilizing Cr2O3 (TXT::wikipedia::Superalloy::002), the diffusion kinetics of Ni in this particular HEA and the precise thickness and uniformity of the enriched layer required for optimal protection are not fully established.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two groups of samples: one subjected to pack cementation to enrich the surface in Ni, and one untreated. Expose both sets to 900 °C in synthetic air for 24 and 48 hours. Analyze the surface oxide composition, morphology, and mass gain.
measurements: Surface composition and oxide phase identification (XRD and EDS)
Oxide scale morphology and adherence (SEM cross-sectional imaging)
Gravimetric mass gain over time
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the Ni-enriched samples do not show statistically significant improvements in oxide layer continuity, lower mass gain, and reduced spallation (compared to untreated samples), then the hypothesis is falsified.

pool.label: C11
pool.builds_on: The paper’s finding that aluminum rapidly oxidizes to form an Al2O3 layer (PMC11169556::web::015) is extended by proposing a controlled pre-formation of this layer to proactively limit degradation.
pool.what_is_new: This hypothesis tests a pre-treatment strategy—in contrast to the in-situ alteration observed by Al addition in the paper—by tailoring the surface oxide through controlled pre-oxidation, specifically aimed at mitigating degradation mechanisms leading to catastrophic failure.

fields.hypothesis: Pre-forming a thin, protective alumina-rich surface oxide can limit degradation by acting as a diffusion barrier that mitigates volatile element depletion at high temperature and reduces the buildup of internal stresses that lead to catastrophic failure.
fields.material_initial_state: Additively manufactured Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 HEA with an as-built fcc matrix microstructure exhibiting a typical AM-induced heterogeneity and without any pre-oxidation treatment.
fields.intervention: Subject the alloy to a controlled low-temperature oxidation step (e.g., 300 °C under low oxygen partial pressure for a short duration) to form a conformal, thin (5–10 nm) alumina-rich surface layer before exposing it to elevated-temperature oxidizing or reducing environments.
fields.conditions: Elevated-temperature exposure (e.g., 400–500 °C) under oxidizing or reducing gas atmospheres after pre-oxidation versus no pre-oxidation; tests performed within the range where diffusion-controlled oxidation is active and before significant phase transformation occurs.
fields.structural_mediator: The pre-formed alumina-rich oxide layer that acts as a barrier to further oxygen ingress and elemental cation outward diffusion.
fields.mechanism: Aluminum has a strong tendency to oxidize and form a stable Al2O3 layer as evidenced in the paper (see PMC11169556::web::015). This thin, dense oxide layer slows down further oxygen influx and retards rapid outward diffusion of other elements. By limiting differential diffusion and elemental depletion (especially of Cr and Ti that aggregate stress during oxidation), the pre-formed barrier minimizes the formation of stress concentrations and microcracks that trigger catastrophic failure.
fields.predicted_outcome: Compared to a baseline with no pre-oxidation, the pre-treated samples will exhibit a more uniform and adherent oxide scale and delayed onset of catastrophic spallation or cracking, thereby extending the operational life under high-temperature exposure; the improvement may be moderate, though exact magnitude is uncertain.
fields.baseline: Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 alloy directly exposed to high-temperature oxidizing or reducing conditions without pre-oxidation yields a non-uniform, layered oxide with elemental depletion zones and premature catastrophic failure.
fields.boundary: Tested over exposure durations (e.g., 30–120 min at 400–500 °C) and oxygen partial pressures in the range of a few to 10 mbar; the hypothesis is applicable as long as the pre-formed layer remains intact and does not itself transform significantly.
fields.uncertainty: While supporting evidence for Al2O3’s barrier properties exists, the interplay with the additive manufacturing microstructure and the Ti content may lead to complex, localized variations in oxide adhesion that require clarification.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of samples: one set receiving the low-temperature pre-oxidation treatment and the other kept as-built. Expose both sets to identical high-temperature (e.g., 450 °C) oxidizing and reducing gas environments under controlled oxygen partial pressures. Monitor the oxide scale formation (by TEM/APT) and perform mechanical testing (e.g., bend or fatigue tests) to detect the onset of spallation and crack formation.
measurements: Oxide scale thickness and uniformity via TEM and APT
Surface composition profiles (EDS/XPS)
Mechanical integrity tests (crack propagation, spallation analysis)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the pre-oxidized samples do not show a statistically significant improvement in oxide scale uniformity, reduced elemental depletion, and delayed catastrophic failure compared to untreated samples, the hypothesis is falsified.

pool.label: C12
pool.builds_on: observations in the paper linking increased porosity with degradation (PMC10820071::web::010::3_2_oxidation_and_phase_transformations_) and the general understanding of corrosion initiation at surface defects (TXT::wikipedia::Corrosion::000).
pool.what_is_new: This hypothesis innovates by applying a post-build laser remelting step to an additively manufactured fcc HEA, directly targeting surface processing defects as a means to limit localized oxidation and subsequent catastrophic failure—a strategy not addressed in the original work.

fields.hypothesis: Post-build laser surface remelting that heals surface defects will reduce localized oxidation pathways, diminishing oxidation-induced stress concentrations and delaying catastrophic failure in the alloy.
fields.material_initial_state: As-built additively manufactured Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 alloy with an fcc matrix that exhibits inherent surface roughness, micro-porosity, and melt-pool boundaries acting as preferential sites for oxygen ingress.
fields.intervention: Apply a controlled post-build laser surface remelting treatment to smooth and homogenize the surface (reducing near-surface porosity and eliminating processing defects) without significantly altering the bulk microstructure.
fields.conditions: Exposure at elevated temperatures (800–950°C) under oxidizing gas (and to a comparative extent, under reducing conditions) for durations sufficient to develop observable oxide scales.
fields.structural_mediator: Reduction of surface defects minimizes fast diffusion paths for oxygen ingress, leading to the formation of a thinner, more uniform oxide scale confined to the surface rather than penetrating into the bulk.
fields.mechanism: Surface defects such as pores and melt-pool boundaries typically act as initiation sites for rapid and localized oxidation. By healing these defects through laser remelting, the pathway for oxygen diffusion is curtailed, thereby reducing the formation of internal oxidation-induced stresses. This control lessens the likelihood of abrupt stress localization and subsequent catastrophic failure.
fields.predicted_outcome: Laser-remelted samples will show lower surface roughness, reduced oxide scale thickness, more uniform oxide coverage, and improved high-temperature mechanical performance (e.g., higher creep or tensile strength and delayed crack initiation) compared to as-built samples.
fields.baseline: As-built samples with untreated surfaces that develop non-uniform oxide scales with localized oxidation penetrating along defects, resulting in earlier mechanical degradation.
fields.boundary: The effectiveness of this intervention is expected in scenarios where oxidation kinetics are active (approximately 800–950°C) and under oxidizing conditions; benefits may be less pronounced in reducing environments where oxidation is minimal.
fields.uncertainty: The precise control of laser remelting to ensure defect elimination without adversely affecting the bulk microstructure remains challenging, and the direct correlation between reduced defect density and oxidation inhibition needs further quantification.

falsification_experiment.design: Fabricate two sets of additively manufactured samples from the same batch: one set receives post-build laser surface remelting and the other remains as-built. Expose both sets to 900°C in air for a fixed time. Characterize surface morphology (using SEM and AFM), quantify oxide scale thickness and uniformity (cross-sectional SEM/EDS), and assess mechanical properties via tensile or creep tests.
measurements: Surface roughness (AFM/SEM analysis)
Oxide scale thickness and uniformity (SEM cross-sectional mapping)
Porosity measurements (micro-CT or SEM image analysis)
Mechanical performance retention (creep life or tensile strength metrics)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the laser-remelted samples do not exhibit statistically significant improvements in surface quality, oxide scale uniformity, reduced oxidation penetration, or mechanical integrity compared to as-built samples, then the hypothesis is falsified.

pool.label: C13
pool.builds_on: The findings from the powder metallurgy HEA work (PMC10650386) regarding microstructural features and oxidation, combined with principles from stainless steel behavior (TXT::wikipedia::Stainless_steel::022) that stress the importance of diffusion paths along boundaries.
pool.what_is_new: This hypothesis directly targets the microstructural attributes unique to AM-produced fcc HEAs—namely, the columnar, high-angle grain boundaries—and proposes grain-boundary modification via homogenization annealing as a means to reveal the role of intergranular oxidation, which was not addressed in the referenced powder metallurgy study.

fields.hypothesis: Grain Boundary Oxidation at Columnar fcc Grain Boundaries Controls Degradation and Catastrophic Failure in AM HEAs.
fields.material_initial_state: The additively manufactured Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 alloy exhibits a columnar, textured fcc grain structure with open, high‐angle grain boundaries inherited from rapid solidification during AM.
fields.intervention: Apply a post-build homogenization annealing treatment designed to promote slight grain growth and reduce high-angle boundary density, thereby reducing fast oxygen diffusion channels along grain boundaries.
fields.conditions: Elevated-temperature exposure (e.g., 850–950 °C) in both oxidizing and reducing atmospheres for durations relevant to service conditions.
fields.structural_mediator: The nature and chemistry of grain boundaries, especially the ease of oxygen ingress along high-angle boundaries in the columnar fcc microstructure.
fields.mechanism: In the as-built AM microstructure, high-angle grain boundaries act as rapid diffusion paths for oxygen (or reactive species in reducing gases), promoting localized intergranular oxidation. This leads to formation of brittle oxide phases or depletion of key alloying elements at the grain boundaries that weaken intergranular cohesion, ultimately causing catastrophic intergranular cracking. Homogenization annealing can modify the grain boundary characteristics to be less ‘open’ and reduce diffusion kinetics along these interfaces.
fields.predicted_outcome: Annealed samples are expected to display a reduced depth of intergranular oxidation, lower formation of deleterious oxide phases along the boundaries, and improved mechanical resistance against catastrophic failure compared with as-built samples. The improvement is predicted qualitatively; quantitative differences would be determined by oxide penetration depth and mechanical testing.
fields.baseline: As-built AM samples with a pronounced columnar, high-angle grain boundary structure that permits rapid gas ingress and subsequent intergranular oxidation.
fields.boundary: The mechanism is expected to dominate degradation at service temperatures where grain boundary diffusion is significant (approx. 850–950 °C) and for exposure durations long enough to allow intergranular oxidation but short enough that bulk recession does not override the boundary effects.
fields.uncertainty: While the direction of improvement is supported by diffusion theory, the precise quantitative change in oxidation depth and mechanical performance is uncertain.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of AM HEA samples: one left as-built and another subjected to a controlled homogenization anneal aimed at modifying the grain boundary structure. Expose both sets to 900 °C in oxidizing (or reducing) atmosphere for a fixed time period. Use cross-sectional EBSD and SEM/EDS analyses to characterize grain boundary oxidation and perform mechanical tests (e.g., fracture toughness) on both sets.
measurements: Grain boundary character distribution (via EBSD).
Oxide scale depth and intergranular oxidation features (via SEM/EDS).
Mechanical strength and fracture toughness post-exposure.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If homogenized samples do not show a statistically significant reduction in intergranular oxidation depth and no improvement in mechanical properties compared to as-built samples, then the hypothesis that grain boundary oxidation governs degradation is refuted.

pool.label: C14
pool.builds_on: The approach leverages established principles from high-temperature oxidation of stainless steels (TXT::wikipedia::Stainless_steel::022) and applies them to the unique AM HEA context.
pool.what_is_new: This hypothesis introduces the concept of reactive element doping (with yttrium) into an AM fcc HEA to tailor the oxidation behavior and mitigate catastrophic failure—a strategy not explored in the referenced powder metallurgy work.

fields.hypothesis: Reactive Element Doping (Yttrium) Enhances Oxide Scale Adherence and Mitigates Gas-Induced Degradation.
fields.material_initial_state: The as-built AM Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 exhibits an fcc matrix with a naturally forming, but potentially non-protective, oxide scale during high-temperature gas exposure.
fields.intervention: Introduce a small quantity (e.g., 0.2–0.5 atomic %) of yttrium into the alloy composition during the AM process, ensuring uniform distribution.
fields.conditions: Expose both Y-doped and undoped AM samples to elevated temperatures (850–950 °C) in oxidizing and reducing gas atmospheres for controlled durations.
fields.structural_mediator: The composition and adhesion quality of the oxide scale formed on the alloy surface and at sub-surface grain boundaries.
fields.mechanism: Yttrium is known to segregate to oxide-metal interfaces and improve oxide scale adhesion by reducing the mobility of the scale and suppressing volatile oxide formation. In the AM HEA, where the natural oxide may spall or permit further gas ingress, Y doping can lead to the formation of a more adherent, protective oxide layer that inhibits rapid oxygen diffusion (or reactive gas interaction in reducing environments). This reduction in oxide scale degradation reduces the risk of catastrophic failure due to spallation-induced surface cracking or internal oxidation.
fields.predicted_outcome: Y-doped samples are expected to form a more uniform and adherent oxide scale with slower growth kinetics. This should result in lower overall degradation rates and delayed onset of catastrophic mechanical failure compared to undoped samples. The qualitative improvement is anticipated; exact quantitative differences in scale thickness or mechanical properties would need experimental determination.
fields.baseline: The undoped as-built AM HEA which develops a less adherent oxide scale under high-temperature exposure, thereby leading to accelerated degradation and failure.
fields.boundary: The effect is primarily relevant under conditions where oxide scale adherence critically influences degradation kinetics (typical for 850–950 °C exposures), and where the Y addition does not adversely impact the primary fcc phase stability.
fields.uncertainty: Although the beneficial effects of Y in oxide scale adhesion are well established in other high-temperature alloys, the magnitude of improvement in the specific AM HEA system remains to be quantified.

falsification_experiment.design: Fabricate two groups of AM HEA samples: one as the baseline and one with 0.2–0.5 at.% Y addition. Subject both groups to high-temperature exposure (e.g., 900 °C) in a controlled oxidizing environment for a fixed time. Characterize the oxide scale using SEM/EDS, measure weight gain (oxidation kinetics), and test mechanical properties post-exposure.
measurements: Oxide scale morphology and thickness (via SEM).
Adhesion quality of the scale (via scratch testing or thermal cycling).
Weight gain per unit area (oxidation rate) and mechanical testing (tensile/fracture tests).
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If Y doping does not yield a statistically significant improvement in oxide scale adherence (thinner, more uniform scale) and no improvement in mechanical integrity under high-temperature exposure compared to undoped samples, the hypothesis is refuted.

pool.label: C15
pool.builds_on: The paper highlighted the significance of dislocation networks and nano-oxides in governing deformation and strength at high temperatures (PMC7229066::web::010, PMC7229066::web::016), suggesting that these features can be critical to degradation if further oxidized.
pool.what_is_new: This hypothesis proposes that internal oxidation along defect structures, modulated by dislocation density, is the critical pathway for high-temperature degradation and catastrophic failure, and it suggests post-processing dislocation reduction as a potential mitigation route—a concept not explored in the original paper.

fields.hypothesis: Catastrophic failure during high-temperature exposure is promoted by stress-assisted internal oxidation along pre-existing dislocation networks, where local oxidation preferentially occurs along these high-energy defect paths, leading to localized embrittlement and crack initiation.
fields.material_initial_state: As-built, SLM-fabricated Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 HEA featuring a high dislocation density and cellular/columnar microstructural features with nano-oxides decorating the substructure.
fields.intervention: Implement a post-processing annealing heat treatment designed to reduce the dislocation density without significantly coarsening the grains, then compare high-temperature degradation behavior between high and reduced dislocation density samples.
fields.conditions: Exposure in either a moderately oxidizing or neutral environment at temperatures of 750–900 °C, where oxygen availability is sufficient for internal oxidation along defects.
fields.structural_mediator: Dislocation network density and the extent of internal oxidation along these networks.
fields.mechanism: High dislocation densities provide rapid diffusion pathways and high-energy sites that facilitate internal oxidation. Under elevated temperature exposure, oxygen penetrates the alloy along these dislocation networks, causing local oxidation that weakens the matrix. This oxidation along defect paths eventually triggers localized crack initiation and propagation, leading to catastrophic failure. A reduction in dislocation density via appropriate annealing would limit these fast-diffusion paths and thus delay degradation.
fields.predicted_outcome: Annealed samples with lower dislocation density should display reduced internal oxidation along former dislocation channels, improved high-temperature mechanical performance, and delayed crack initiation compared to as-built high dislocation density samples. Microstructural characterization (using TEM and ECC imaging) should reveal fewer oxidized channels in the annealed specimens.
fields.baseline: The as-built alloy with high dislocation density exhibits internal oxidation along dislocation networks, contributing to earlier catastrophic failure under high-temperature exposure.
fields.boundary: The hypothesis is intended for high-temperature regimes (750–900 °C) under conditions where oxygen is present at levels that promote internal oxidation but do not immediately result in complete external oxidation.
fields.uncertainty: While the role of dislocation networks and nano-oxides is supported by the paper (see PMC7229066::web::010 and PMC7229066::web::016), the quantitative effect of dislocation density reduction on internal oxidation in this specific composition remains to be fully elucidated.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of samples: one set remains as-built, and the other is annealed under conditions optimized to reduce dislocation density while preserving grain size. Expose both sets to high-temperature (e.g., 800 °C) in a controlled atmosphere with moderate oxygen partial pressure. Characterize the extent of internal oxidation (using TEM/ECC imaging) and evaluate mechanical performance (via compressive or creep testing).
measurements: Dislocation density via XRD or TEM
Extent and morphology of internal oxidation along defect paths
Mechanical strength and time-to-failure data
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the annealed (lower dislocation density) samples do not exhibit a significant reduction in internal oxidation along defect paths or do not show improved high-temperature mechanical properties compared to the as-built samples, the hypothesis is falsified.
